extracted.intended_audience: practitioners, judges, and students of United States patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts standards and doctrinal criteria governing infringement, injunctions, interferences, and the nature of invention under U.S. patent law as summarized in a legal treatise index. Useful for applying or evaluating claims, remedies, and procedural prerequisites in patent litigation and Patent Office contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territoriality of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringing acts (making, using, or selling) are generally actionable only when done in the United States; use abroad or on foreign vessels and use in England of articles purchased abroad are not (or present limits on) U.S. infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts done on American vessels may be treated differently; making or sale in the U.S. for use abroad or on foreign vessels is treated specially (see cited authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may commit acts of infringement (liable parties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide range of actors can commit infringement: private individuals, co-owners, licensees, assignees, officers and employees of corporations, municipal and public corporations in certain circumstances, contractors, agents, salesmen, workmen, partners, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special rules apply to government entities (United States cannot commit infringement in ordinary fashion); municipal corporations, public corporations, and corporations acting through agents are treated with nuanced liability rules (see citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of the United States and public corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States cannot commit infringement in the ordinary sense; claims against the U.S. must be urged in the Court of Claims; public corporations and municipal bodies have distinct rules on liability depending on benefit and control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the government obtains the entire benefit of the infringement or municipal corporations take benefit from departments over which they have no control, liability may attach; contractors and contractors' acts treated differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee liability and scope of license
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee acting within the scope of an express license generally cannot be held to infringe; departure from the license, violation of license restrictions, or sales to persons without a right to use can create infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues include express vs implied licenses, license rescission, practice of licensee's own invention, effect of non-payment of royalties, post-expiration acts, and whether license was ever valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary liability/contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Making or selling articles or materials intended to be united with others or sold for use in a patented art can amount to infringement depending on intent and use; sale of materials to be used in the art may be actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplying one element with intent that it be combined with others can infringe; the line between innocent supply and contributory infringement depends on intent and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agents, contractors, and intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Common carriers, custom-house agents, contractors, salesmen, agents, and servants may be implicated in infringement, but liability depends on collusion, active participation, or notice; involuntary acts of workmen are generally not infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transporting in collusion with an infringing seller is culpable; acts of agents of public boards or corporate officers may bind their principals when the entity is enjoined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patents — use of different or fewer elements
rubrics_metrics.description: For combination patents, use of different elements, fewer elements, a different grouping, or elements selected from several combinations is generally not an infringement of the claimed combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitution of newly discovered elements, adding elements, or using elements for new purposes raises nuanced questions; mere suggestion by the patented combination does not make a different combination an infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unclaimed elements and sub-combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of unclaimed elements or sub-combinations is not necessarily infringement; infringement is more likely where any claimed element is used or where an element invented by the patentee is used contrary to the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether use of an unclaimed element infringes depends on claim scope and whether the element is a material part of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-element patents and combination use
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent on an element may be infringed by its use in a combination; conversely, a patent to a combination may give rise to infringement claims against makers of an element when intended for use in the patented combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination focuses on the role of the element in producing the claimed result and intent to induce combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing infringement and single-act presumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain infringing acts may be continuing; however, one act of infringement is not presumed from another, and use of less than all steps (in process claims) may not constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing character affects remedies and injunctions; courts examine whether repeated or continuous acts are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-infringing-process rule limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a product made by an infringing art is not always itself infringement of the art patent (distinctions exist between product, process, and manufacture patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether use or sale of a product made by an infringing process infringes depends on the type of patent (art, machine, manufacture, composition, design) and claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies — availability and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies for infringement include legal and equitable relief but are not always complete; patentees may resort to various means (including discovery) to detect infringement; federal courts have jurisdiction for actions for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies include damages, profits, accounting, injunctive relief; some remedies may be waived or limited depending on plaintiffs' pleadings (e.g., remedy in assumpsit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages and evidence standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages (and implied damages) arise from infringement; evidence for damages and infringement may include inferential evidence but accidental infringement must be clearly proved; one act is not presumed from another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh evidence carefully; rules on admissibility and inferences are developed in cited authorities (1041–1048, 1127 n.2, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment and transfer of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights of action for infringement are assignable with the patent but require distinct words of conveyance; assignments can transfer claims including those of expired patents depending on wording and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal conveyancing language is required to transfer infringement causes of action; nuances exist for expired patents and transferred suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of the infringer in law and equity
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringer is a tortfeasor at law but in equity may be treated similarly to a trustee; this shapes remedies, obligations, and equitable relief available against infringers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable doctrines (accounting, constructive trusts, etc.) may apply, but courts recognize limits to equating infringers to trustees in all respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction in patent cases aims to prevent infringement and avoid multiplicity of suits; it protects the patentee's rights where other relief is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injunctions serve both preventive and protective functions and are discretionary equitable relief governed by established principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites for granting an injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will grant injunctions only when requisite equitable conditions are met: patent validity, title in plaintiff, danger of infringement, irreparable injury threatened, and inadequacy of legal remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court's discretion is governed by equitable principles; injunctions are not granted to punish past wrongs or to compel settlements; the plaintiff must show need and proper purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of prior judgments and public acquiescence as evidence of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior judgments, public acquiescence, and admissions of defendant are important evidence of a patent's validity; prior judgments of high courts are strongest but are conclusive only when issues, parties, and evidence align.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public acquiescence is measured by degree and duration; prior judgments from different parties/issues carry less weight and may be rebutted by new evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: When injunctions will not be granted
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunctions are denied when other adequate relief exists, the defendant can no longer infringe, the plaintiff has laches or unreasonably acquiesced, the plaintiff never used the invention, enforcement would work injustice, or validity is doubtful/conflicting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denial also arises where defendant acted in good faith and invested large sums, where granting would coerce unrelated matters, or where the patent is recent/reissue appears too broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of hardships and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider business interests of both parties and public consequences; severe consequences to the defendant or public may weigh against an injunction even where the plaintiff has rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff is clearly entitled to an injunction the defendant's business interests may be disregarded, but public necessity (e.g., public works) can limit relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond, account, and substitute relief in lieu of injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may require bond of indemnity or order an accounting and bond in lieu of a prohibitory injunction in appropriate cases (e.g., defendant has large stakes, patent about to expire, plaintiff guilty of laches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In clear cases bond and account are not substituted; substitution is discretionary and depends on equities like priority doubts and defendant status (vendee, contractor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties against whom injunctions can issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunctions may issue against manufacturers, sellers, users, assignees, grantees, licensees exceeding license, agents, officers, corporations, public and private bodies, and co-owners when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain exceptions apply: not issued against licensees who innocently exceed scope and stop on notice, not issued against representatives of deceased infringers unless they also infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, scope, and duration of injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction may be preliminary or perpetual, unconditional or on terms, tailored to the case, confined to intended purposes, may limit prohibition to future additions, and has rules about duration, effect outside the court's jurisdiction, modification, suspension, revival on reissue, and dissolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issued by consent, no other questions are decided; courts may fit injunctions to particular facts and can modify or suspend as equity requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for motions for injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions for injunctions in federal courts generally require notice to defendants, may be preceded by restraining orders, allow appearances and answers, involve evidence admissible at motion stage, and may lead to contested hearings or sending issues to a jury or master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte relief is exceptional; courts examine only enough to determine necessary protection on motion and rely on obvious facts rather than extended hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt, enforcement, and penalties for violating injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation of an injunction constitutes contempt unless obeyed until rescinded; courts may order attachment, set penalties, and exercise subsequent control; knowledge of injunction is equivalent to notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant's good faith or advice of counsel is not a complete excuse though it may affect penalty; contempt proceedings follow equitable and procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of injunctions on appeals and judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant or refusal of injunctions is discretionary and not always appealable; reversal affects enforcement and penalties; injunctions are not superseded by appeal in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal procedures and effects depend on whether questions of law are involved and the stage of proceedings; reversal may alter contempt or enforcement consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference proceedings purpose and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Interferences in the Patent Office are contests over priority between pending applications or between pending applications and unexpired patents; priority is the sole question and proceedings deal with applications rather than applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interferences are instituted only where claims conflict (identical, equivalent, or one embracing another) and are governed by rules different from court litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution and jurisdiction of interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner (and Patent Office examiners) have jurisdiction over whether an interference should be declared; the primary examiner first decides whether applications conflict; the decision to declare is final as to necessity for institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interferences may be instituted nunc pro tunc in certain cases and have special prerequisites for pending applications and unexpired patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference procedure and preliminary statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference proceedings require preliminary statements, notices to rival claimants, completion of specifications when conflict discovered, filing and amendment rules, and allowance for inspection of files and conflicting specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary statements have formal requisites; failure to file can have serious effects (judgment for failure); amendments and disclaimers are treated specially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and weight of proof in interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: A party asserting priority must affirmatively establish it; proof need not remove every reasonable doubt, but the weight required against an applicant must be such as would defeat the patent in the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules of evidence and burden largely follow court practice (e.g., District of Columbia rules) with certain special rules in the Patent Office; technical objections and motions to suppress are governed by examiner practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment, appeal, and effect of interference determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment of priority in an interference may be rendered on evidence, concession, or written abandonment and is conclusive unless appealed; interference judgments are evidence of priority but are not always binding on courts as to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal from interference decisions has limits; the judgment's weight depends on issues, parties, and evidence; estoppel rules and the possibility of reopening on new evidence exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and essential attributes of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention is defined by essential attributes: not every new thing is an invention; it must be the product of inventive skill, useful, and must produce physical effects; invention may be an art or an instrument but not a mere principle or function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essence of an invention is ascertained by assigning it to its proper group (force applied, mode of application, specific treatment) and by looking at the want it satisfies; unity and subordinate relationships matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception vs reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception of an invention is not complete until reduced to practice; reduction to practice occurs when the invention is actually practised (not merely contemplated or experimented upon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception without reduction is insufficient for priority; simultaneous conception issues and reduction-to-practice timing are critical in disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity and equivalence in invention and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity and equivalence are assessed by identity of force, object, and mode of application; equivalence exists when the same means produce the same effect; whether inventions are identical or diverse is a fact question and claims govern determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific versus generic differences, differences in form, materials, arrangement, or use, and whether one embodiment can substitute for another are analyzed; claims control scope and equivalence analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest, disclosure, and nature of patent privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent law balances inventor's right with public interest; immediate disclosure is important, the patent confers a limited monopoly but promotes public welfare by encouraging inventions; property in invention consists of the exclusive right to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication under American law and the duty of disclosure are emphasized; the nature and scope of invention and patent privilege must align with public policy.
